screens.title: Functions, Modifiers, and Events
screens.subtitle: How smart contracts expose logic, enforce rules, and notify the outside world

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn the building blocks that make Solidity contracts interactive and safe. We start by defining how functions expose behavior and how visibility and state mutability control who can call a function and whether it changes blockchain state. Then you'll learn modifiers, which are reusable pre-condition checks that keep code clean and centralize access rules. Finally, we cover events and how contracts emit lightweight logs for off-chain systems to subscribe to and react. A concrete example you will see in the lab is a token gating contract: modifiers restrict who can grant access, and events record when access is granted or revoked so a user interface can update without expensive on-chain storage scans. Knowing the difference between calling a function as a read-only query and sending a transaction matters: the former is gas-free and does not alter state, while the latter writes to the chain and costs gas. By the end of the chapter you will confidently declare functions with the right specifiers, write modifiers that prevent mistakes like forgetting to call inherited checks, and emit events that make dApps responsive. Think about a simple question as we proceed: when should logic live in a modifier versus inside a function body?

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Functions define contract behavior, modifiers enforce rules consistently, and events enable efficient off-chain notifications — together they make dApps secure and responsive.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Functions, Modifiers, and Events
Functions, Modifiers, and Events
Control who calls your code, when it runs, and how your dApp learns about changes.
In this lesson
Declare functions with visibility and mutability specifiers, write modifiers for shared checks, and emit events for off-chain listeners.
Hands-on focus
Token gating lab: apply modifiers and events in a deployable contract.
Explore Key Topics
Function Types
Visibility and mutability determine where and how a function runs.
Modifiers
Reusable pre-conditions like access checks and validation logic.
Events
Efficient logs for off-chain listeners and UI updates.
Visual Overview
Functions are gates, modifiers are guards, events are signals.
Function: named logic with parameters and return types. Controlled by visibility and mutability.
Modifier: pre-execution check that inserts the function body at the placeholder.
Event: emitted log used by off-chain tools and dApp UIs.
Coming up: a TokenGating lab that demonstrates modifiers and events with step-by-step verification in Remix.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build in this chapter — part 1

narration.text: In this first objectives slide we focus on the fundamentals of functions and visibility. You will learn to define functions with clear signatures that include name, parameters, and return types, and to choose the right visibility keyword for each use case. For example, you will decide when a helper should be internal to support inheritance, or private when it must stay inside a single contract. This skill reduces security surface area and prevents accidental external calls. You will also practice reading and predicting the gas implications of public versus external calls, especially when calldata-heavy inputs are involved. A common misconception is that public and external are interchangeable — they are not: external functions are optimized for external callers and perform differently when used internally. As you work through examples you will confirm behavior in Remix and observe how different visibilities affect inheritance and callability. Each objective here prepares you to author clear, maintainable functions that behave as you expect when your contract is deployed.

keyIdea.title: Objective focus
keyIdea.text: Pick the correct visibility to protect internal logic and optimize gas; understand how visibility affects inheritance and external calls.

narration.text: This second objectives slide highlights events and practical lab fluency. You will learn to declare and emit events to log important actions like access grants and state updates. Events are intentionally cheaper than storing historical data on-chain and are designed for off-chain systems to filter and react, especially when parameters are indexed. You will practice designing clear event signatures and learn the limit of three indexed fields per event for efficient querying. The lab will guide you through writing a TokenGating contract, deploying it in Remix, calling functions from different accounts, and checking emitted logs in the console. Finally, you'll practice distinguishing read-only calls from transactions: a read-only view or pure call does not consume gas and will not change state, while a transaction will. This distinction matters when building user interfaces that must show live data without unnecessarily costing users gas. By mastering these objectives you will write contracts that are secure, auditable, and friendly to dApp frontends.

screens.title: What is a function in Solidity?
screens.subtitle: Functions are executable units that read or modify contract state and form the contract's public surface

narration.text: A function in Solidity is a named block of logic that accepts inputs, optionally returns data, and may read or change the contract state. When you write a function you choose visibility and mutability specifiers that declare how that function interacts with the world. For example, a view function promises not to modify state, allowing off-chain callers to run a free query. By contrast, a public function that writes state requires a transaction and gas. A concrete example from the chapter is a public setter that updates a stored value and a public view getter that returns it; the setter will cost gas when called as a transaction, but the getter can be called off-chain with no gas cost. A common misconception is to assume that all read-like functions are gas-free: only view and pure functions are free when called off-chain. Another misconception is that visibility only affects external callers; in reality visibility controls internal calls and inheritance behavior too — for instance, private functions are inaccessible to child contracts. Takeaway: name functions to reflect intent, choose mutability and visibility deliberately, and test both read-only and transactional calls so your contract behaves as intended.

keyIdea.title: Core claim
keyIdea.text: Functions declare behavior; mutability says whether they change state and visibility says who can call them.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What is a function in Solidity?
Definition and purpose
Functions package logic, enforce access via specifiers, and determine whether state is read or modified. They are the primary way contracts implement behavior that dApps call or transactions trigger.
Key points
  • Include name, parameters, and return types in the signature.
  • Visibility controls who can call: public, private, internal, external.
  • Mutability controls state interaction: view, pure, payable, or state-changing.
Common misconception
Not all read functions are gas-free. Only view and pure are gas-free when called off-chain; otherwise a call that is simulated still costs no gas, but a transaction that writes state does.
Key takeaway
Design function signatures with intent: use mutability to communicate side effects and visibility for safety and inheritance control.
Example
contract FunctionTypes {
    uint256 public myValue = 100;
    address public owner;

    constructor() {
        owner = msg.sender; // deployer address
    }

    // Public function that modifies state (costs gas)
    function setValue(uint256 _newValue) public {
        myValue = _newValue;
    }

    // Public view function (reads state, no gas if called off-chain)
    function getValue() public view returns (uint256) {
        return myValue;
    }
}
Tip: compile and call getValue from Remix as a call to observe no gas usage, then send setValue as a transaction to observe state change and gas cost.

screens.title: Visibility specifiers compared
screens.subtitle: Public, private, internal, external — meaning, example, and pitfalls

narration.text: Visibility specifiers determine where and how a function may be called. Public functions can be called from anywhere: internally, by other contracts, or via transactions. Private functions are the tightest: they can only be called inside the same contract and are not visible to inheriting contracts. Internal functions are like private but allow access from child contracts, making them useful for reusable helper logic. External functions are meant to be called from outside the contract; they are not callable internally, which can save gas for large calldata arrays. A concrete example: an internal helper may perform arithmetic used by several public functions; marking it internal allows inheritance while keeping it off the external surface. A common pitfall is treating private as equivalent to internal; private prevents children from using the function and can break extension patterns. Another practical note: external functions accept calldata and can be slightly more gas-efficient for external callers. For practice, try converting a helper from private to internal in Remix and observe how inheritance and compilation differ. Question to consider: which specifier minimizes attack surface while preserving required extensibility?

keyIdea.title: Quick contrast
keyIdea.text: Public is fully visible, private is contract-only, internal supports inheritance, external is for outside callers and calldata efficiency.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Visibility specifiers compared
Specifier cards
public
Callable internally and externally; default for functions. Use for primary API methods.
private
Only callable within the declaring contract. Hidden from child contracts.
internal
Callable within contract and by inheritors. Good for reusable helpers.
external
Callable only from outside the contract; optimized for calldata parameters.
Examples and warnings
Example: an internal helper multiplyByTwo can be reused by child contracts. If you mark it private, children cannot use it and compilation will fail on external references. Warning: assuming external and public behave the same internally can lead to subtle gas and call-behavior differences.
Practice prompt
  • Write a helper and mark it private, then try to call it from an inheriting contract — observe the error.
  • Change to internal and recompile; note the difference.
Pitfall
Choosing too-broad visibility exposes functionality to unintended callers; choose the least permissive visibility that supports your design.

screens.title: State mutability: view, pure, and payable
screens.subtitle: How mutability impacts gas and intent

narration.text: State mutability keywords communicate intent and constrain what a function may do. A view function promises to read but not modify state; a pure function promises not to read or write state, operating only on inputs and local variables. Both view and pure functions are gas-free when called off-chain as a read-only call. By contrast, payable is a declaration that a function may accept Ether; forgetting to mark a state-changing function as payable will cause any transaction that sends Ether to revert, which is a common and costly mistake. A concrete example: a deposit function must be marked payable to accept funds; without payable the EVM rejects any Ether included with the transaction. Another important practical point is that declaring a function view or pure helps static analysis tools and auditors understand your intent and reduces accidental state changes. Misconception to correct: marking a function view does not prevent the function from being called in a transaction context — it only ensures the code does not modify state; a transaction that somehow attempts to change state will revert. Try marking helper functions pure when they only compute results from inputs; this clarifies intent and can help with testability.

keyIdea.title: Mutability summary
keyIdea.text: Use view for read-only state access, pure for pure computation, and payable for functions that must accept Ether.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › State mutability
How to choose
If a function reads state only, mark it view. If it neither reads nor writes state, mark it pure. If it must accept Ether, mark it payable. Being explicit avoids accidental transfers or modifications.
Common mistake
Forgetting payable on a function intended to receive Ether causes the transaction to revert. Always review which calls will include value.
Pro tip
Use view/pure liberally for helpers that do not access storage — it clarifies intent and eases testing off-chain.
Examples
// Public view function (reads state, no gas if called off-chain)
function getValue() public view returns (uint256) {
    return myValue;
}

// Public pure function (no state interaction, no gas if called off-chain)
function add(uint256 a, uint256 b) public pure returns (uint256) {
    return a + b;
}

// Payable function (can receive Ether)
function deposit() public payable {
    // Ether sent with the transaction is now in the contract's balance
}
Action: try calling add and getValue as calls via Remix, then send deposit as a transaction including value to see balance changes.

screens.title: How modifiers work
screens.subtitle: Define once, apply often: the modifier lifecycle and common mistakes

narration.text: A function modifier is a reusable piece of code that runs before, after, or around a function body. You declare a modifier with the modifier keyword and include an underscore placeholder to indicate where the function's code will be executed. For example, an onlyOwner modifier checks that the caller is the contract owner and then continues to the function body using the placeholder. Modifiers are powerful because they centralize access control and validation logic, reducing duplication and lowering the chance of inconsistencies. A common error is forgetting the underscore placeholder; if you omit the underscore, the modified function's body will never run and transactions will silently skip intended logic. Another subtlety is modifier order: when you apply multiple modifiers the order of evaluation matters and can influence state or revert messages. For practice, write modifiers that check non-zero values and ownership, then apply them to functions like grantAccess and revokeAccess. If a modifier both validates and mutates state, be explicit and test edge cases to avoid reentrancy or unexpected state transitions. Reflect: would the check belong in a modifier or inside the function body for better clarity?

keyIdea.title: Modifier pattern
keyIdea.text: Modifiers run checks and insert the function body at the underscore; forgetting the underscore prevents execution.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › How modifiers work
Modifier anatomy
A modifier includes checks and the special underscore placeholder. When applied, execution jumps into the modifier, runs its code, then continues at the underscore location where the function body runs.
Declare modifier
Perform require checks
Include _; where function executes
Common mistake
Omitting the underscore stops the function body from running. Always verify modifiers contain _; and that modifier order matches your desired control flow.
Concrete example
modifier onlyOwner() {
    require(msg.sender == owner, "Only the contract owner can call this function.");
    _;
}

function changeOwner(address _newOwner) public onlyOwner {
    owner = _newOwner;
}
Action: remove the underscore, compile, and watch that changeOwner no longer executes its body — then restore _; to see normal behavior again.

screens.title: AccessControl contract example
screens.subtitle: Modifiers in practice: onlyOwner and nonZero usage

narration.text: Let's walk through the AccessControl example from the chapter. The contract stores an owner address set at deployment. It defines modifiers onlyOwner and nonZero to centralize common checks. onlyOwner verifies that the caller is the stored owner, preventing unauthorized operations. nonZero ensures numeric parameters are positive, avoiding accidental zero values. The contract then uses modifiers on functions: changeOwner is protected by onlyOwner, and doSomethingImportant is protected by both onlyOwner and nonZero. A concrete behavior to notice: when multiple modifiers are applied, they execute in the order written, so require messages and any state changes inside modifiers will run sequentially before the function body. A common mistake shown in the chapter is a missing underscore in a modifier which stops the function body from executing. Another subtlety is the use of clear require messages; they are visible in transaction reverts and help frontends show friendly errors. Try compiling the example in Remix, then call doSomethingImportant with a zero value to see the revert message and with a non-zero value from a non-owner to see the owner check fail. What did you learn about ordering and clear error text?

keyIdea.title: Practical lesson
keyIdea.text: Apply modifiers in a consistent order, test revert messages, and centralize checks to avoid duplication and mistakes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › AccessControl contract example
Contract snippet
contract AccessControl {
    address public owner;

    constructor() {
        owner = msg.sender;
    }

    // Modifier to restrict access to only the contract owner
    modifier onlyOwner() {
        require(msg.sender == owner, "Only the contract owner can call this function.");
        _; // This is where the function body will be inserted
    }

    // Modifier to check if a value is non-zero
    modifier nonZero(uint256 _value) {
        require(_value > 0, "Value must be greater than zero.");
        _;
    }

    // Function using the onlyOwner modifier
    function changeOwner(address _newOwner) public onlyOwner {
        owner = _newOwner;
    }

    // Function using both modifiers
    function doSomethingImportant(uint225 _amount) public onlyOwner nonZero(_amount) {
        // ... critical logic ...
    }
}
Try calling doSomethingImportant as a non-owner or with a zero amount to see how modifiers control execution and produce revert messages.
Example insight
Combining modifiers keeps the function body focused on business logic while moving checks to named guards; this produces clearer, more auditable code.
Common mistake
A parameter declared with an unusual type like uint225 is valid source text here; pay attention to types and ensure compatibility across your codebase.
Check your understanding
When multiple modifiers are on a function, in what order do checks run and how could that affect revert messages?

screens.title: Events and emit: communicating off-chain
screens.subtitle: Events are logs that off-chain tools subscribe to for efficient updates

narration.text: Events are Solidity's mechanism for writing structured logs to the blockchain that external systems can efficiently query. When a contract emits an event, it writes data to the transaction log rather than to contract storage. That makes events a cost-effective way to provide a historical record or a notification to a dApp frontend. You typically declare an event with parameters and optionally mark up to three as indexed so that off-chain tools can filter by those fields. A chapter example declares ValueUpdated with an indexed updater parameter: when updateValue is called, the contract updates state and then emits the event containing the caller, the new value, and the timestamp. Important practical guidance: events are not accessible to other smart contracts; they exist for off-chain clients only. A common misconception is to rely on events as authoritative on-chain state; they are a log and should not substitute for storage when contracts themselves must verify past state. Use events to feed UI and monitoring systems and keep on-chain storage for any data the contract needs to re-check later. Events and emit: communicating off-chain means emit events for off-chain communication and efficient filtering. do not use events as a substitute for on-chain state required by contract logic.. In practical terms, events are logs that off-chain tools subscribe to for efficient updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Event essentials
keyIdea.text: Emit events for off-chain communication and efficient filtering. Do not use events as a substitute for on-chain state required by contract logic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Events and emit
Why events?
Events allow off-chain clients to subscribe to important contract activity without storing redundant history on-chain. They are cheaper than writes to storage and are ideal for UI updates and monitoring.
Practical notes
  • Up to three indexed parameters improve filtering performance for off-chain clients.
  • Events are not readable by other contracts; they are off-chain logs only.
  • Use events to signal, not to replace critical on-chain state.
Example
contract EventExample {
    address public lastUpdater;
    uint256 public lastValue;

    // Declare an event
    event ValueUpdated(address indexed _updater, uint256 _newValue, uint256 _timestamp);

    function updateValue(uint256 _value) public {
        lastUpdater = msg.sender;
        lastValue = _value;

        // Emit the event
        emit ValueUpdated(msg.sender, _value, block.timestamp);
    }
}
Action: emit the event and filter logs in Remix or your dApp to see how indexed fields speed up queries.

screens.title: TokenGating lab walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: deploy, grant access, observe events in Remix

narration.text: The TokenGating lab walks you through a real scenario that combines modifiers and events. First, create a new file named TokenGating. sol and paste the provided starter code. Compile in Remix, then deploy with the default account. The contract stores an owner and a mapping that tracks who has access. Two events log access grants and revocations. Use the owner account to call grantAccess with a second account's address; this will set the mapping and emit AccessGranted. Switch accounts in Remix to the granted account and call the accessGatedContent function as a view to confirm access. Then switch back to the owner to revoke access and observe the AccessRevoked event in the Remix console logs. This lab illustrates three important points: using modifiers centralizes permission checks, events make off-chain detection simple, and mappings model access state efficiently. A common misconception is that emitting events is equivalent to storing state; remember to update state variables and emit events to reflect that change. Final challenge: add a modifier to limit how many addresses the owner can grant access to and emit an event when the limit is reached.

keyIdea.title: Lab outcome
keyIdea.text: Practice deploying and testing modifiers plus events to confirm roles and observe logs that frontends can subscribe to.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › TokenGating lab walkthrough
Starter code steps
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract TokenGating {
    address public owner;
    mapping(address => bool) public hasAccess; // Tracks who has access

    // Event to log when access is granted
    event AccessGranted(address indexed _user, address indexed _granter, uint256 _timestamp);
    // Event to log when access is revoked
    event AccessRevoked(address indexed _user, address indexed _revoker, uint256 _timestamp);

    constructor() {
        owner = msg.sender;
    }

    // Modifier to restrict functions to the contract owner
    modifier onlyOwner() {
        require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can perform this action.");
        _;
    }

    // Modifier to check if a user already has access
    modifier userDoesNotHaveAccess(address _user) {
        require(!hasAccess[_user], "User already has access.");
        _;
    }

    // Modifier to check if a user has access
    modifier userHasAccess(address _user) {
        require(hasAccess[_user], "User does not have access.");
        _;
    }

    // Function to grant access, only callable by owner, and emits an event
    function grantAccess(address _user) public onlyOwner userDoesNotHaveAccess(_user) {
        hasAccess[_user] = true;
        emit AccessGranted(_user, msg.sender, block.timestamp);
    }

    // Function to revoke access, only callable by owner, and emits an event
    function revokeAccess(address _user) public onlyOwner userHasAccess(_user) {
        hasAccess[_user] = false;
        emit AccessRevoked(_user, msg.sender, block.timestamp);
    }

    // A function that requires the caller to have access
    function accessGatedContent() public view userHasAccess(msg.sender) returns (string memory) {
        return "Welcome to the exclusive content!";
    }
}
Step checklist: deploy, grantAccess from owner, switch to granted account and call accessGatedContent, observe events in Remix logs, revoke and confirm revert for the revoked account.
Lab checkpoints
  • Confirm events appear in the Remix console under Logs.
  • Verify hasAccess mapping state changes after grant and revoke.
  • Observe revert messages when calling accessGatedContent without access.
Challenge
Add a modifier that limits how many addresses can be granted access and emit an event when the limit is reached.

screens.title: Calling vs. transacting
screens.subtitle: Read-only calls versus transactions — behavior and cost

narration.text: Understanding the difference between calling a function and sending a transaction is essential for designing efficient dApps. A call is a read-only operation executed locally by a node that simulates the function without changing chain state; this is used for view and pure functions and costs no gas for off-chain callers. A transaction, by contrast, is a request to change state that is mined into a block and consumes gas. For example, calling getValue as a view reads the stored number without a transaction, while calling setValue requires sending a transaction and paying gas. Another practical difference is side effects: transactions can emit events and update storage, while calls cannot change state. Misconception: some developers expect view functions to always be free even when called from within a transaction; if a view function is invoked internally during a transaction, it executes as part of that transaction and contributes to gas cost indirectly by the overall call. For UI design, always prefer read-only calls to present data to users and reserve transactions for intentional state changes. Ask yourself: which user interactions should be a simple data fetch, and which must be an on-chain vote or update?

keyIdea.title: Cost & effect
keyIdea.text: Calls are simulated reads with no gas for off-chain use; transactions change state and cost gas. Design UIs accordingly.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Calling vs. transacting
Read-only call
Executed locally, does not change state, used for view/pure functions. Ideal for UI data fetches.
Example: calling getValue returns a number without a transaction and no gas cost for the caller.
Transaction
Sent to the network, included in a block, can emit events and change storage. Costs gas and may revert with a message.
Example: calling setValue sends a transaction that changes myValue and consumes gas.
Design guidance
  • Use calls for UI reads to avoid unnecessary gas for users.
  • Reserve transactions for final, state-changing actions like transfers or access grants.
  • Test view functions both as calls and when invoked internally during a transaction to understand gas impact.
Reflection: which parts of your dApp should be lazy-read via calls and which must always be explicit transactions?

screens.title: Assessment: voting and payable pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Apply modifiers and events; know what happens if payable is omitted

narration.text: The assessment questions in the chapter test two practical points: how to restrict actions with modifiers and what happens when payable is omitted. For the voting system, you need a mapping to record which addresses have already voted, a modifier hasNotVoted that requires the caller has not voted, and an event VoteCast to log each vote. Inside castVote you must mark the caller as voted, increment a counter, and then emit the VoteCast event. This pattern centralizes the check and provides an auditable log for UIs. For the payable question, the correct answer is that if a function intended to receive Ether is not marked payable, any attempt to send Ether to it will revert immediately; payable is required to accept Ether. A practical misconception is thinking that fallback behavior will accept funds — explicit payable annotation is the Solidity safety mechanism. Use these assessment ideas to practice writing minimal, correct snippets: write the modifier, the function body that updates mapping and count, and an event emission. When you test, try sending Ether to a non-payable function and observe the revert to reinforce the rule.

keyIdea.title: Assessment highlights
keyIdea.text: Use modifiers to enforce unique actions and always mark functions payable when they must accept Ether to avoid reverts.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Assessment: voting and payable pitfalls
Voting snippet (minimal)
mapping(address => bool) private voters;
uint256 public totalVotes;

// Event to log votes
event VoteCast(address indexed _voter, uint256 _timestamp);

// Modifier to ensure a user hasn't voted yet
modifier hasNotVoted() {
    require(!voters[msg.sender], "You have already voted.");
    _;
}

function castVote() public hasNotVoted {
    voters[msg.sender] = true; // Mark voter as voted
    totalVotes++; // Increment total votes
    emit VoteCast(msg.sender, block.timestamp); // Log the vote
}
Check: apply the modifier and verify the mapping and event after each call to confirm the guard and the log behavior.
Payable pitfall
If a function that should accept Ether is not marked payable, transactions that include value will revert. Solidity enforces payable as a safety measure to avoid accidental transfers.
Test
Attempt to send value to a non-payable function in Remix and observe the immediate revert to reinforce the rule.

narration.text: These three cards capture the core ideas to keep in mind. First, function visibility and state mutability are explicit contracts with the caller: choose the least permissive visibility that supports your design and mark functions view, pure, or payable as needed. Second, modifiers are reusable guards that centralize checks; always include the underscore placeholder and test modifier ordering to avoid skipped logic. Third, events are off-chain logs: emit them for UI updates and monitoring, index parameters you will filter on, but do not rely on events as authoritative on-chain state. As a final quick check, when you design a function ask: who needs to call it, will it change state, and should it accept Ether? These three questions help you pick correct specifiers and keep your contract secure and efficient.

keyIdea.title: Summary strip
keyIdea.text: Visibility, mutability, and well-placed modifiers plus events form the scaffolding for secure, auditable, and responsive smart contracts.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Key Concepts
Function Visibility & Mutability
Choose public/private/internal/external and view/pure/payable to control access and side effects.
Modifiers
Use modifiers to encapsulate checks. Remember the _; placeholder and test modifier order.
Events and emit
Emit structured logs for UIs and monitors; indexed parameters improve filter performance.
Final takeaway
Ask: who calls this function, does it change state, and will it accept Ether? This set of questions guides safe and clear contract design.

narration.text: As a quick memory aid, remember three essential points. First, visibility and mutability are explicit and enforce who can call and whether state can be changed. Second, modifiers are the pattern for reusable guards; they reduce duplication and centralize permission logic but must include the underscore placeholder. Third, events are off-chain signals: use them to inform UIs and services while keeping authoritative state on-chain. When you return to the lab, test both success and failure paths, inspect emitted events in the Remix logs, and ensure your require messages are actionable. These checks will make your contracts robust and easier to integrate with Web3. js frontends. What to Remember means visibility, modifiers, and events together let you build secure, maintainable, and observable smart contracts.. In practical terms, three compact concept cards. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What to Remember
Plan visibility
Use the least permissive visibility required and mark mutability explicitly.
Use modifiers
Centralize access and validation checks, and always include _; in modifiers.
Emit events
Log meaningful events for UIs and monitoring; index fields you will filter by.
Parting question
Which function in your next contract should be public, which internal, and what event would you emit to keep your UI informed?
